Nineteen chapters in four parts, one part for each phrase of the subtitle, *Applications of Lidar, Radar and Optical Data in Forest Mensuration, Landscape Monitoring and Greenhouse Gas Inventory*.

Chapter titles were rewritten on 5 September 2026 against the contents pages of *Satellite Remote Sensing for Forest and Environmental Monitoring* (Elsevier Earth Observation Series, 2025), where every title opens on the operation rather than the topic, names the sensor, and lands a result. Section headings were rewritten the same day into the same register, Title Case noun phrases of at most three words. Neither set has been written into the manuscript, and both are here for review.

At the 6 September revision 11 of the then seventeen chapters were drafted and 159 sections were written. Two chapters entered the outline on 10 September 2026, the risk mapping chapter at the end of Part 3 and the disturbance disaggregation chapter at the end of the book, and neither has sections drafted yet. Sections marked *track* are verification tracks, unnumbered and unlisted in the book itself, and a reader who skips every one of them still gets a complete book. At the pace of the comparable series volume, 20 chapters over 663 pages, nineteen chapters runs to about 630 pages before front matter.

# Notes on this revision

**Chapter 2** was drafted on 5 September 2026 and renders in both formats. Nine sections, 3,814 words of prose, and every number in the prose is computed by a chunk on the page. It retires the existing raster chapter when promoted.

**Chapter 1** exists as a skeleton, carrying its section headings and the argument each must make, with prose only where the argument is settled.

**Chapter 3** is the only gap. Nothing in the library carries radar, the title promises it, and it is the largest single piece of new writing in the book.

**Chapters 6, 8, 9 and 15** are new chapters whose source material exists elsewhere in the library and has never been written up as teaching.

**Chapters 14 and 19** entered the outline on 10 September 2026 from the brief at `publishing/chapter-briefs/risk-and-disaggregation.md`, and their source material is in the library.

The spine was amended on 5 September 2026. The closing message of the book is disturbance ecology, and the spatio-temporal data cube is the instrument that makes it arguable rather than the destination. The final part takes up bifurcation and tipping behaviour, regime shift in forest carbon flux, and Markov chain Monte Carlo as the machinery for inference about a dynamical system observed with error. The disturbance disaggregation chapter, added as the last chapter on 10 September 2026, now owns that argument.
